source_title: 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan Summary and Framework
finding: The DROA Target Elevation of 3,525 ft was deliberately set 35 ft above minimum power pool (3,490 ft) to create an operational response window — enough time and elevation buffer to mobilize DROA releases and adjust GCD monthly volumes before the dam loses hydropower generation capability or the Upper Basin violates Colorado River Compact delivery obligations.
why_it_matters: The 35-ft buffer between 3,525 ft and 3,490 ft is the entire operational window for DROA to work; if Lake Powell reaches 3,525 ft and DROA measures take months to deliver water, every foot of this buffer matters for whether hydropower generation and compact compliance can be maintained.
condition_or_trigger: Lake Powell elevation approaching or projected to fall below 3,525 ft above mean sea level — the DROA-defined Target Elevation that triggers drought response action
evidence_quote: The operating principle of DROA is to minimize the risk of Lake Powell falling below a minimum 'Target Elevation,' expressly defined as a water surface elevation of 3,525 ft. The Target Elevation was adopted to 'minimiz[e] the risk of Lake Powell declining below minimum power pool (approximately elevation 3,490 feet msl) and to assist in maintaining Upper Division States' compliance with the Colorado River Compact.'
notes: First-pass extraction; requires sampled human review before dataset release.

source_title: Inferred inflow forecast horizons guiding reservoir release decisions across the United States
finding: A study across 300+ US dams found that approximately 80% of large US reservoirs (≥10 Mm³ storage) use medium-to-long range inflow forecasts to inform release decisions during at least part of the water year. Western high-elevation reservoirs — including large Colorado River system dams — rely on long-range forecast horizons (>6 weeks) driven primarily by snowpack information.
why_it_matters: Establishes that the 24-Month Study's integration of CBRFC snowpack-based inflow forecasts into Lake Powell release scheduling is standard operational practice for large western reservoirs — not an exceptional feature. This supports interpreting the 24-Month Study as the operational norm rather than a conservative workaround.
condition_or_trigger: Standard reservoir operating conditions at large US dams using seasonal snowpack information to inform release decisions, particularly during winter and spring runoff periods
evidence_quote: We estimate that approximately 80 % of large dams and reservoirs in the US (1553± 50 out of 1927 dams with at least 10 Mm3 storage capacity) adopt medium- to long-range inflow forecasts to inform release decisions during at least part of the water year. Long-range forecast horizons (more than 6 weeks ahead) are detected in the operations of reservoirs located in high-elevation regions of the western US, where snowpack information likely guides the release.
notes: First-pass extraction; requires sampled human review before dataset release.

source_title: Circle of Blue: Glen Canyon Dam faces its existential moment
finding: Glen Canyon Dam has three water release pathways with distinct critical elevations: (1) spillways at 3,648 ft (irrelevant at current water levels); (2) eight 15-ft diameter penstocks that cease operating below 3,490 ft minimum power pool; and (3) four 8-ft diameter river outlet works at elevation 3,370 ft, functionally limited at 3,394 ft, not designed for full-time use, and which suffered cavitation damage during the 2023 high-flow experiment.
why_it_matters: The three-pathway structure defines a precise hydraulic ladder of failure: 3,490 ft ends hydropower; below that, the outlet works carry the entire water release burden but are structurally at risk and undersized for compact obligation deliveries. The 2023 cavitation event provides direct evidence that the outlet works are not a reliable full-time substitute for the penstocks.
condition_or_trigger: Lake Powell declining below minimum power pool elevation (3,490 ft), requiring full reliance on river outlet works for all water releases — a condition that Reclamation's 2024 technical memo explicitly warns against
evidence_quote: The main exit point is through the eight penstocks, the 15-foot diameter tubes that move water through the turbines to generate hydroelectricity. The penstocks are incapacitated when Powell drops below 3,490 feet. [...] If that happens, water must be released through four 8-foot diameter pipes called the river outlet works. Smaller than the penstocks, the river outlet works are located at elevation 3,370. Below that elevation water cannot be released from Powell, a status known ominously as 'dead pool.' (Functionally, the river outlet works may be useless at elevation 3,394.)
notes: First-pass extraction; source is credible media reporting on Reclamation's own technical memo findings. Verify outlet works elevations against official technical memo before final dataset release.

source_title: Circle of Blue: Glen Canyon Dam faces its existential moment
finding: Reclamation has established 3,500 ft as its operational redline for Lake Powell — 10 ft above minimum power pool — because it cannot reliably operate the river outlet works for extended periods. However, this redline effectively strands 4.4 MAF of Lake Powell storage (only 3.7 MAF is hydraulically accessible), preventing compact-obligation deliveries from that volume.
why_it_matters: The 3,500 ft operational floor is not a formal rule but an engineering judgment call; it creates a de facto dead pool 10 ft higher than the legal minimum power pool, stranding a volume of water roughly equal to two-thirds of one year's typical Lake Powell release. This stranded volume is what motivates lower-basin stakeholders to push for dam infrastructure modifications.
condition_or_trigger: Inability to reliably operate river outlet works for sustained periods when Lake Powell is below 3,500 ft — an infrastructure limitation identified in Reclamation's March 2024 technical memo
evidence_quote: Because Reclamation is not confident it can operate the river outlet works for an extended run, the agency is focused on keeping Powell above elevation 3,500 feet. Protecting 3,500 feet comes with all sorts of baggage. It preserves hydropower generation, which power customers appreciate. But in effect the redline at that elevation strands some 4.4 million acre-feet in Lake Powell. (Only 3.7 million acre-feet is technically accessible with the current plumbing.)
notes: First-pass extraction; source attributes 3,500 ft operational focus to Reclamation. Verify the 4.4 MAF and 3.7 MAF figures against official technical documentation before final dataset release.

source_title: Circle of Blue: Glen Canyon Dam faces its existential moment
